title: Thomas and the Wounds
subtitle: The Man Who Needed to Touch
author: YourWord

paragraphs.body: Thomas was not there the first time. The other ten disciples were locked in a room on the evening of the resurrection, doors shut, afraid of what the authorities would do next. Jesus came and stood among them and showed them his hands and his side and breathed on them and gave them the Holy Spirit. It was the most significant moment in the history of the movement they had all given years to. Thomas missed it completely.

The others found him and told him: we have seen the Lord. Ten people who had known Thomas for years, who had walked the same roads and eaten the same meals and watched the same miracles, were all telling him the same thing. He looked at all of them and said: unless I see the nail marks in his hands, and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.

He was specific about what he needed. Not a feeling. Not a vision. Not someone's testimony. The actual wounds. His finger in the actual holes. His hand in the actual side. Thomas had watched Jesus die. He had seen what Roman crucifixion does to a body up close. Whatever he was going to believe had to be able to account for that. He was not being stubborn. He was being precise.

A week passed. Thomas stayed with the group. He did not leave. He was present the following Sunday when they were gathered again behind locked doors. Jesus came through the locked doors again and stood in the middle of the room. He looked directly at Thomas. He said: put your finger here. See my hands. Reach out your hand and put it into my side. Stop doubting and believe. He had heard exactly what Thomas said a week ago.

The text does not say whether Thomas actually touched the wounds. It moves straight to his response. He said: MY LORD AND MY GOD. Eight words that represent the highest confession in the entire gospel of John. Not just teacher. Not just rabbi. Not just the risen one. Lord and God, said by the man the church remembers for doubting, in the moment his doubt ended.

Jesus said: because you have seen me you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed. It was not a rebuke exactly. It was an acknowledgment and then a reach across time to every person who would come after Thomas without the option of locked rooms and visible wounds. Thomas got to see. He said so himself. The rest of the world would have to work with something Thomas never had to.

Thomas went on to take the gospel further east than any other disciple. Tradition says he reached India, planted churches in Kerala, and died there by spear. The man who needed to touch the wounds before he believed carried that belief farther geographically than almost anyone else in the room that night. His doubt did not disqualify him. It just needed a week and a direct answer.
